Chapter 01 · Brief

Material before ornament

A workshop study in joining two unlike materials: a warm, carved teak stock and a precisely fitted mild-steel barrel.

The project was built in the second semester as part of the Workshop and Materials course. A single piece of teak formed the stock; a steel rod formed the barrel. The central challenge was not surface styling, but maintaining one continuous profile while fitting both parts cleanly.

Reference study — the stock, barrel and hardware read as one long, balanced silhouette.

Chapter 02 · Workshop process

Finding the curve by hand

The teak blank was marked, cut and progressively reduced at the bench. A spokeshave replaced the conventional planer for the compound curves: it followed the changing section more closely and made the stock easier to control by hand.

The process moved between outline, vice-held carving and repeated visual checks. Shavings were evidence of reduction; the surface emerged by removing small amounts rather than forcing the final profile at once.

Chapter 03 · Joinery

Fitting wood to steel

The mild-steel rod was seated through a sleeve cut precisely into the stock. The sleeve turned the joint into a controlled mechanical fit rather than an attachment added after the wood was finished.

Alongside the main build, small sheet-metal and wire trials extended the course exploration into cutting, joining and controlled bending.

Chapter 04 · Final model

The finished assembly

The final model holds the grain, tool marks and small asymmetries of a hand-shaped object. Dark-finished teak carries the visual mass; the slender steel barrel extends the line without competing with it.

The project made the lesson physical: tool choice changes the geometry one can achieve. For this stock, the spokeshave proved more effective than a planer because it could stay responsive to a curved surface.
